section.title: David and Jonathan
section.sectionRationale: David has just felled Goliath, and two very different responses form at once. The king’s own son, Jonathan, strips off his robe and armor to give them to David and binds himself to him in covenant love, while the king himself curdles with envy the moment the women sing David’s praise above his own. The chapter tracks both threads together, Saul’s mounting jealousy and repeated attempts to be rid of David by the Philistines’ hand, and the LORD’s unmistakable presence with David through it all, culminating in David’s marriage to Michal. It is one movement: covenant loyalty and royal jealousy rising side by side.
section.thesis: As the LORD’s hand rests visibly on David, the heir to the throne freely yields his own claim in a covenant of love while the reigning king, seeing the same hand, is consumed with a jealousy that will not rest until David is destroyed.
section.frameNote: Four beats: Jonathan’s covenant with David, verses 1 to 4; Saul’s jealousy ignited by the women’s song, verses 5 to 9; the LORD with David while Saul is afraid of him, verses 10 to 16; and David’s marriage to Michal amid Saul’s scheming, verses 17 to 30.

verses.text: After David had finished speaking with Saul, the souls of Jonathan and David were knit together, and Jonathan {{ahav|loved}} him as himself.
And from that day Saul kept David with him and did not let him return to his father’s house.
Then Jonathan made a {{berit|covenant}} with David because he loved him as himself.
And Jonathan removed the robe he was wearing and gave it to David, along with his tunic, his sword, his bow, and his belt.

units.label: Saul’s jealous eye
units.note: what more can he have but the kingdom

verses.text: So David marched out and prospered in everything Saul sent him to do, and Saul set him over the men of war. And this was pleasing in the sight of all the people, and of Saul’s officers as well.

As the troops were returning home after David had killed the Philistine, the women came out of all the cities of Israel to meet King Saul with singing and dancing, with joyful songs, and with tambourines and other instruments.
And as the women danced, they sang out: “Saul has slain his thousands, and David his tens of thousands.”
And Saul was furious and resented this song. “They have ascribed tens of thousands to David,” he said, “but only thousands to me. What more can he have but the kingdom?”
And from that day forward Saul kept a {{qana|jealous}} eye on David.

units.label: The LORD with David, Saul afraid
units.note: the LORD was with David but had departed from Saul

verses.text: The next day a spirit of distress sent from God came upon Saul, and he prophesied inside the house while David played the harp as usual. Now Saul was holding a spear,
and he hurled it, thinking, “I will pin David to the wall.” But David eluded him twice.
So Saul was afraid of David, because the LORD was with David but had departed from Saul.
Therefore Saul sent David away and gave him command of a thousand men. David led the troops out to battle and back,
and he continued to prosper in all his ways, because the LORD was with him.
When Saul saw that David was very successful, he was afraid of him.
But all Israel and Judah loved David, because he was leading them out to battle and back.

Then Saul said to David, “Here is my older daughter Merab. I will give her to you in marriage. Only be valiant for me and fight the LORD’s battles.” But Saul was thinking, “I need not raise my hand against him; let the hand of the Philistines be against him.”
And David said to Saul, “Who am I, and what is my family or my father’s clan in Israel, that I should become the son-in-law of the king?”
So when it was time to give Saul’s daughter Merab to David, she was given in marriage to Adriel of Meholah.
Now Saul’s daughter Michal loved David, and when this was reported to Saul, it pleased him.

“I will give her to David,” Saul thought, “so that she may be a snare to him, and the hand of the Philistines may be against him.” So Saul said to David, “For a second time now you can be my son-in-law.”
Then Saul ordered his servants, “Speak to David privately and tell him, ‘Behold, the king is pleased with you, and all his servants love you. Now therefore, become his son-in-law.’”
But when Saul’s servants relayed these words to David, he replied, “Does it seem trivial in your sight to be the son-in-law of the king? I am a poor man and lightly esteemed.”
And the servants told Saul what David had said.
Saul replied, “Say to David, ‘The king desires no other dowry but a hundred Philistine foreskins as revenge on his enemies.’” But Saul intended to cause David’s death at the hands of the Philistines.
When the servants reported these terms to David, he was pleased to become the king’s son-in-law. Before the wedding day arrived,

David and his men went out and killed two hundred Philistines. He brought their foreskins and presented them as payment in full to become the king’s son-in-law. Then Saul gave his daughter Michal to David in marriage.
When Saul realized that the LORD was with David and that his daughter Michal loved David,
he grew even more afraid of David. So from then on Saul was David’s enemy.
Every time the Philistine commanders came out for battle, David was more successful than all of Saul’s officers, so that his name was highly esteemed.

ahav.gloss: To love, to be bound to another in loyal affection. Jonathan’s love for David, verse 1 and again in verse 3, is not sentiment but covenant loyalty, the same word used of Israel’s love owed to the LORD, Deuteronomy 6:5. The heir to the throne loves the man who will replace him.

berit.gloss: Covenant, a binding, solemn agreement sealed with signs and obligations. Jonathan’s covenant with David, sealed by handing over his robe, armor, sword, bow, and belt, formally surrenders the crown prince’s own claim to the throne in favor of the LORD’s anointed.

qana.gloss: To be jealous, envious, or zealously protective. The same root can describe righteous zeal for the LORD, but in Saul it curdles into a corrosive envy of the very man whose success he cannot deny, verse 9, and it will drive the rest of the book’s conflict.

basic.context: Fresh off David’s victory over Goliath, this chapter follows two threads at once. Jonathan, Saul’s own son and heir, is so bound to David in loyal love that he strips off his royal robe and weapons and gives them to David, sealing a covenant. Meanwhile Saul, hearing the women sing that David has killed his tens of thousands to Saul’s mere thousands, is consumed with jealousy. From that day he watches David with a jealous eye, and it grows into repeated, thinly disguised attempts to have David killed by the Philistines, first through military assignments and then through a bride price of a hundred foreskins. Yet through it all the refrain returns again and again: the LORD was with David. The key questions are why Jonathan would give up his own claim to the throne, and why success that should have brought Saul security instead bred fear and hatred.
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative describing what actually happened at Saul’s court; it is not a manual instructing every reader to make identical covenants or to expect kings’ sons to hand over robes. What the narrative teaches by pattern and repetition is that the LORD’s presence and blessing cannot be manufactured or seized by human striving, and that covenant loyalty, pictured in Jonathan, stands in stark contrast to self-protective envy, pictured in Saul.
basic.originalLanguages: Jonathan’s ahav, love, for David in verse 1 is covenant loyalty, not mere feeling, and it leads him to cut a berit, covenant, with David in verse 3, sealed by the transfer of his own royal garments and weapons. Saul, by contrast, from verse 9 keeps a qana, jealous, eye on David, the same word that can describe holy zeal turned instead into a corrosive envy that will not rest.
basic.typology: Jonathan, the rightful heir, willingly strips off his own royal robe and gives it to David, the anointed but not yet enthroned king, a small but vivid picture of one who yields his own claim so that God’s chosen king may be clothed and honored. It faintly anticipates the self-emptying of the true King who did not grasp His own glory but gave Himself for others.
basic.christ: David is repeatedly described as the man the LORD is with, hated and hunted by the reigning power precisely because of that presence, yet prospering in everything and beloved by the ordinary people even as the establishment turns against him. He is anointed but not yet enthroned, a pattern the New Testament shows fulfilled in Jesus, who was with the Father’s favor upon Him, opposed by the rulers of His day, and vindicated not by seizing a throne but by receiving one from the Father in due time.
basic.god: God is the one whose invisible presence is the true engine of the whole chapter; every success of David’s is traced to the LORD being with him, and every fear of Saul’s is traced to the LORD having departed from him. God sovereignly protects His anointed even through a jealous king’s repeated Philistine ploys, showing that human hostility cannot thwart what God has purposed.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Samuel 16:13-14 records the Spirit coming upon David and departing from Saul, the hinge this chapter plays out. Philippians 2:5-8 pictures Christ emptying Himself as Jonathan foreshadows in miniature. Proverbs 27:4 warns that jealousy is more dangerous than wrath, exactly what unfolds in Saul.
basic.oneStory: David the shepherd, already anointed in secret, now begins the long road of being loved by some and hunted by others precisely because the LORD is with him, one more link in the chain that leads from the promise of a king from Judah to the greater Son of David, Jesus, who is beloved of the Father, opposed by rulers, and finally given the everlasting throne.

context.literary:
The chapter is stitched together by a single repeated phrase functioning almost as a chorus: the LORD was with David, verses 12, 14, and 28, each time set directly against Saul's fear. A reader who removed every other sentence and kept only that refrain would still understand the chapter's argument, which is exactly the narrator's point; the political and domestic events are commentary on a spiritual reality, not the other way around.

The chapter also frames itself with two very different acts of giving. It opens with Jonathan stripping off his own robe, tunic, sword, bow, and belt to hand them to David, a costly, willing surrender, verses 3 to 4. It closes with Saul demanding a bride price of a hundred Philistine foreskins, a violent, calculated exaction dressed up as generosity, verses 25 to 27. Two kinds of giving bracket the same chapter, one that empties the giver for love and one that uses a gift to destroy its recipient.

Saul's schemes are consistently narrated, then immediately undercut, a technique the author repeats until it becomes almost comic. Saul thinks, I need not raise my hand against him, verse 17; Saul thinks, she may be a snare to him, verse 21; Saul intends David's death by Philistine hands, verse 25; each private calculation is stated openly to the reader and then dismantled within a verse or two by David's unexpected success. The reader is let in on every plot before it fails, which builds an ironic distance between Saul's confidence and the reader's growing certainty that none of it will work.
context.historical:
A victorious army returning home being met by women singing and dancing with tambourines was an established convention, not an invention of this chapter; Miriam leads Israel's women the same way after the sea, Exodus 15:20-21, and Jephthah's daughter greets her father after his own victory the same way, Judges 11:34. What made this occasion combustible was not the custom but the content of the couplet, crediting the newcomer with ten times the king's own tally.

Giving a daughter in marriage as the reward for defeating a feared enemy had precedent in Israel's own conquest traditions; Caleb offers his daughter Achsah to whoever captures Kiriath-sepher, Joshua 15:16-17, so Saul's initial offer of Merab was not an unusual gesture for a king to make to a champion. The customary bride price, mohar, that a groom or his family paid to the bride's father, attested in Genesis 34:12 and legislated in Exodus 22:16-17, is what makes Saul's substitute demand so calculated: he asks for proof of slain enemies instead of silver, turning an ordinary marriage custom into a death sentence dressed as an honor.

Counting slain enemies by a collected body part rather than by name was known practice elsewhere in the ancient Near East, where victory inscriptions sometimes tallied a battle's dead by parts gathered from the field rather than by roll call. Saul's specific demand for a hundred foreskins, doubled by David to two hundred, verse 27, functioned exactly this way, an unmistakable, countable proof that could not be faked or exaggerated.
context.canonical:
The pattern of a rejected or displaced figure turning to murder rather than to repentance did not begin with Saul; Cain's face falls when his offering is not regarded, and sin, crouching at the door desiring him, leads to his brother's death, Genesis 4:3-8. Saul's decline follows the same arc in miniature, envy over an unrewarded comparison curdling toward violence, showing this chapter as one more chapter in a very old biblical story about what jealousy does to a human heart left untended.

The covenant Jonathan seals here, and the love Michal shows David within the same chapter, both bear fruit much later. David's lament over Jonathan calls his love extraordinary, surpassing the love of women, 2 Samuel 1:26, language that only makes sense against everything chapter 18 has already shown of Jonathan's self giving loyalty. Michal's love, noted twice here, verses 20 and 28, later curdles into contempt when David dances before the ark, 2 Samuel 6:16-23, a sour coda to a marriage that began, on her side at least, in genuine affection.

The women's song does not stay confined to Israel. It resurfaces on Philistine lips at Achish's court, 1 Samuel 21:11 and 29:5, evidence that this single chapter's events had already become common knowledge across the border, shaping how both nations would read every step David took from here forward.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author wants two responses to the same evident fact, that the LORD's favor now visibly rests on David, held up side by side so their contrast does all the teaching. Jonathan sees the same success Saul sees and responds with covenant loyalty that costs him his own royal claim; Saul sees it and responds with envy that will cost him everything else. Neither man doubts that David is genuinely blessed; the author is not interested in whether the evidence is clear; he is interested in what each heart does with evidence it cannot deny.

The repeated notice that the LORD was with David also trains the reader to interpret ordinary sounding events, a military promotion, a marriage negotiation, a song at a homecoming, as theological rather than merely political. Nothing that happens to David in this chapter is his own doing in the author's telling; even his successes in battle are attributed to the LORD's presence rather than to skill. The author intends that pattern to carry forward into every later chapter of David's long conflict with Saul: whatever happens next, the reader has already been told who is really at work.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter narrates ancient marriage customs, a bride price, a substitute payment in slain enemies, multiple candidate daughters offered to the same suitor, as historical description of how kings and warriors negotiated marriage in this period, not as models for believers to imitate. Nothing here commends violence as a wedding gift or treats women as prizes to be exchanged; the narrative simply reports what Saul in his corruption actually did and lets the outcome expose him.

What does transfer is the discernment the chapter quietly requires between two things that can look similar from outside: zeal and envy. The same Hebrew root behind Saul's jealous eye, verse 9, can describe righteous zeal for the LORD elsewhere in Scripture, so believers cannot simply avoid all strong feeling about another's success; they must ask whether their intensity protects what is right or resents what is another's. Saul's history answers that question for him by where his jealousy leads.

debates.question: Why did Jonathan give up his own claim to the throne so readily?

views.label: Recognition of the LORD's choice
views.case: Jonathan already knew, or came to know, that the LORD had chosen David; his covenant is a faith-filled acceptance of God's sovereign choice over his own dynastic ambition.

views.label: Personal loyalty and affection
views.case: The text emphasizes that Jonathan loved David as himself; the covenant flows first from deep personal affection and only implicitly from awareness of David's future kingship.

debates.bearing: Either way, Jonathan models a self-giving loyalty that refuses to grasp at what is not his, in sharp contrast to his father's grasping fear.

debates.question: Was Saul's jealousy inevitable given his earlier rejection, or a fresh moral failure?

views.label: The fruit of a heart already turned from God
views.case: Since the Spirit had departed from Saul, chapter 16, his jealousy is the natural fruit of a heart no longer anchored in trust in the LORD.

views.label: A fresh, culpable choice
views.case: Saul is not merely a passive victim of his earlier rejection; each new act, from throwing the spear to plotting the Philistine trap, is a fresh, willful sin for which he remains responsible.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree that Saul is genuinely guilty; the chapter never excuses him even while showing the spiritual roots of his decline.

study.originalLanguages:
Beyond ahav, berit, and qana already named, four more words shape how this chapter wants to be heard.

David's repeated success is described with sakal, verses 5, 14, 15, and 30, a verb whose range covers both to act wisely and to prosper or succeed, the same duality found in the Hebrew of Isaiah 52:13, where the LORD's Servant will act wisely and, in the same word, be raised and lifted up and highly exalted. The narrator is not simply saying David kept winning; he is saying David kept acting with a wisdom that God rewarded with success, exactly the pattern Isaiah later gives the Servant.

Saul's response is tracked through yare, afraid, in an escalating sequence: he is afraid of David because the LORD had departed from him, verse 12; he is afraid of him because David was very successful, verse 15; and finally he grows even more afraid, verse 29, each occurrence marking a further collapse rather than a resolution of the fear. The verb never resolves into courage or repentance; it only intensifies.

The bride price Saul demands is called mohar, verse 25, the ordinary legal term for what a groom paid a bride's family, attested the same way in Genesis 34:12 and Exodus 22:16-17. Saul's twist is not the custom but the currency, substituting silver or livestock with a hundred Philistine foreskins, orlah, verse 25, the same root that names the mark of covenant exclusion mocked in Goliath's own title the chapter before, this uncircumcised Philistine, 1 Samuel 17:26. The chapter closes an earlier insult by turning the very thing that marked Philistines as outside the covenant into the bloody proof David must bring back, doubled, verse 27, to enter Saul's own family.

One ordinary verb quietly holds the whole chapter's contrast together: natan, to give. Jonathan gives, natan, his robe and weapons to David out of love, verse 4. Saul then gives, the same verb, his daughter Merab to Adriel instead of David, verse 19, gives orders to his servants to speak to David privately, verse 22, and finally gives Michal to David only once the bloody bride price is paid, verse 27. The narrator lets one plain verb carry both a covenant of self-giving love and a king's calculated, weaponized generosity, so that by the chapter's end the reader has learned to ask, every time someone gives something in this book, what it is actually meant to cost the receiver.

typology.type: Jonathan stripping off his own royal robe, tunic, sword, bow, and belt to give them to David
typology.fulfillment: A crown prince voluntarily hands over the visible signs of his own claim and his own means of self-defense to the man who will replace him, keeping nothing back, verse 4. This anticipates Christ, who though existing in the form of God did not consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, Philippians 2:6-7. Jonathan loses a throne he never occupies; Christ lays aside a glory He eternally possessed, so the pattern is real but the cost in Jonathan's case is only ever a possibility, while in Christ's case it is an actual, historical self-emptying.

typology.type: David marked out again and again as the LORD's beloved yet hunted by the reigning power that should have welcomed him
typology.fulfillment: Every success in this chapter is credited to the LORD's presence with David even as the man who anointed him king in Israel's eyes turns against him, verses 12 to 15. This foreshadows Jesus, publicly named My beloved Son in whom I am well pleased, Matthew 3:17, yet handed over by the very religious authorities who should have recognized Him, John 1:11. In both cases visible divine favor provokes opposition rather than welcome from the established power, a pattern Scripture treats as normal rather than surprising for God's anointed.

typology.type: Saul's fury at a song that exalts a rival above him, though the rival has done nothing but serve faithfully
typology.fulfillment: David gives Saul no cause for offense; the women's arithmetic alone ignites an envy that has been waiting for any excuse, verses 8 to 9. Matthew records almost the identical dynamic at Jesus' trial: Pilate knew that it was out of envy that they had handed Jesus over to him, Matthew 27:18, the chief priests moving against a man whose only offense was drawing greater acclaim than the establishment could tolerate. Saul's jealousy previews, in miniature, the very motive the Gospels name for the cross itself.

typology.type: A figure who acts wisely and succeeds under hostility long before he is finally exalted
typology.fulfillment: The verb behind David's repeated success and the verb behind Isaiah's Servant who will act wisely and be highly exalted share the same Hebrew root, sakal, Isaiah 52:13. David prospers under Saul's growing opposition well before he ever wears a crown, just as the Servant's exaltation follows, rather than avoids, a season of being despised and rejected, Isaiah 53:3. The correspondence is linguistic and thematic rather than a direct prophecy, but it traces the same divine pattern: faithful wisdom under pressure precedes public vindication.

study.christ:
The shape of Saul's opposition in this chapter, an escalating sequence that never quite succeeds, previews something larger than one king's failure. Saul moves from a private jealous eye, verse 9, to a battlefield assignment meant to expose David to Philistine swords, verse 13, to a marriage trap meant to finish what the battlefield could not, verses 17 and 21, each stage more calculated than the last and each stage strengthening David rather than destroying him. The opposition to Jesus follows a similar widening arc, from murmuring crowds to plots by night to a cross meant to end Him permanently, yet at every stage what was intended to destroy Him instead accomplished the Father's saving purpose, this Man was delivered up by God's set plan and foreknowledge, and you, by the hands of lawless men, put Him to death, Acts 2:23.

Saul's bride price is the clearest single picture. A gift disguised as an honor is actually engineered to kill the man who accepts it, verse 25; David not only survives it but doubles the payment and gains the very alliance Saul hoped would undo him, verse 27. Centuries later Joseph will name this exact reversal for his own suffering, you intended to harm me, but God intended it for good, Genesis 50:20, and the cross is the ultimate instance of it: the very instrument gathered to destroy God's Anointed becomes the means of the world's redemption.

Jonathan's covenant, meanwhile, offers the chapter's gentlest picture of Christ. He surrenders what is rightfully his, asks nothing back but loyal love, and binds himself permanently to a king he did not have to serve, verses 3 to 4. That is a small, real anticipation of a King who gave up everything that was rightfully His, and who binds Himself to His people not because they have anything to offer Him but because He has chosen to love them, laying down His own royal claim not to a rival but for the sake of those who could never have earned His allegiance.
study.god:
God's presence and absence are this chapter's real subject, and the narrator makes no attempt to hide that fact behind political explanation. Every one of David's successes is explicitly credited to the LORD being with him, verses 12, 14, and 28, and every one of Saul's fears is explicitly credited to the LORD having departed from him, verse 12. The chapter offers no other cause for either man's trajectory; skill, popularity, and royal favor all appear on the surface, but the narrator insists the deeper current is the presence or absence of God Himself.

God's patience with Saul is also on display, even if it is easy to miss beside the drama of David's rise. Saul is not struck down for throwing a spear or for plotting murder by proxy; he is simply, repeatedly, thwarted, allowed to keep scheming while none of his schemes land. That restraint is itself a kind of mercy, giving Saul chapter after chapter to turn back before his final end, even while making unmistakably clear that his throne will not pass to his own line.

God is also shown here as the true source of the covenant loyalty Jonathan displays. Jonathan's love is called ahav, the same root Israel is commanded to feel toward the LORD Himself, Deuteronomy 6:5, which means the chapter is quietly teaching that human loyalty at its best is patterned after, and sourced in, God's own covenant faithfulness rather than being a purely human virtue Jonathan simply happens to possess. What Jonathan gives to David, God gives, in far greater measure, to everyone bound to His Anointed.

Finally, God's sovereignty extends here even into the currency of violence Saul chooses. A bride price meant to kill instead becomes proof of victory and the doorway into the royal family; nothing Saul arranges, however carefully, escapes being turned toward the very outcome he is trying to prevent.

crossReferences.note: The Spirit of the LORD rushes upon David at his secret anointing in the same breath that it departs from Saul. Every later notice in this chapter that the LORD was with David, and every notice that Saul was afraid, is simply this earlier hinge working itself out in public view.

Cain's face falls when his offering goes unregarded, and unaddressed resentment leads him to murder his own brother. Saul's jealousy over an unfavorable comparison follows the identical arc, envy left untended hardening from a wounded ego into a settled intention to destroy the one who provoked it.

Caleb offers his daughter Achsah in marriage to whoever captures Kiriath-sepher, an older instance of the very custom Saul corrupts here, rewarding a warrior's victory with a daughter's hand. Saul takes an honorable precedent and turns it into an assassination plot.

The law's ordinary provision for a bride price, mohar, paid by a groom to a bride's family, is the very custom Saul weaponizes by substituting a hundred Philistine foreskins for silver, turning a protective legal provision into a death warrant dressed as an honor.

My Servant will act wisely, He will be raised and lifted up and highly exalted uses the same Hebrew root translated prospered of David throughout this chapter, tracing a shared pattern of wise, faithful success under pressure that culminates, far more fully, in the Servant's exaltation.

Pilate knew it was out of envy that the chief priests had handed Jesus over, the same corrosive comparison that seizes Saul when the women's song exalts David above him. Jealousy of a rival's God-given success, not any real offense, drives both plots.

Peter tells Jerusalem that Jesus was delivered up by God's set plan and foreknowledge even though lawless hands crucified Him, the same pattern this chapter shows in miniature: human schemes meant for harm, like Saul's, end up serving purposes their plotters never intended.

Christ, existing in the form of God, empties Himself and takes the form of a servant before being highly exalted, the pattern Jonathan's surrendered robe and weapons dimly rehearse when a rightful heir gives away his own claim out of love rather than losing it by force.

Love does not envy stands as a direct verdict on Saul's condition in this chapter; whatever loyalty or admiration he once had for David has curdled into the one thing real love, by definition, cannot hold alongside itself.

study.oneStory:
The whole Bible keeps returning to a single choice, whether to trust and love what God is doing even when it costs us our own place, or to grasp at status and destroy whoever threatens it. Jonathan and Saul embody both options inside one family in a single chapter: a son who releases his claim to the throne out of love for God's anointed, and a father who would rather use his daughter as bait than accept that the kingdom is passing to someone else. Scripture keeps replaying that same fork in the road, from Cain and Abel to the chief priests and Jesus, because it is the same fork every generation faces.

This chapter also advances the specific covenant thread that began with David's private anointing, chapter 16, and will run for the rest of Samuel and beyond. Jonathan's covenant of loyal love here is renewed and deepened in chapter 20, invoked again when David shows kindness to Jonathan's crippled son for Jonathan's sake, 2 Samuel 9, and echoed in David's own grief when Jonathan finally falls, 2 Samuel 1:26. A promise made in one chapter, under real danger and real cost, is kept faithfully for decades, which is exactly the kind of loyalty the Bible asks its readers to recognize as a reflection of God's own character.

The chapter closes with David more loved by the ordinary people and more hated by the reigning power than at any point so far, verses 16 and 29, a tension the rest of Scripture does not resolve quickly. It resolves only in great David's greater Son, likewise beloved of the Father and opposed by the rulers of His day, whose apparent defeat at the hands of jealous authorities becomes, in God's hands, the means by which an everlasting, unshakeable throne is finally established, not for one family only but for everyone bound to Him in covenant love.

quiz.q: What did Jonathan do to seal his covenant with David?

options.text: He gave David his own robe, tunic, sword, bow, and belt.
options.note: Verse 4 records this costly, symbolic transfer of the prince’s own royal and military gear.

options.text: He simply promised David his friendship in words.
options.note: There were words of love, verses 1 and 3, but the covenant was sealed with a concrete, costly act, not words alone.

options.text: He asked Saul’s permission before befriending David.
options.note: No such request is recorded; the covenant is Jonathan’s own initiative toward David.

options.text: He challenged David to a contest of arms.
options.note: The opposite happened; Jonathan surrendered his own arms to David rather than contesting him.

quiz.q: What sparked Saul’s jealousy of David in this chapter?

options.text: The women’s song crediting David with tens of thousands and Saul with only thousands.
options.note: Verses 7-9 show this exact song is what turned Saul’s heart toward envy.

options.text: David’s marriage to Michal.
options.note: The marriage comes later and deepens Saul’s fear, but the jealousy began earlier, with the victory song.

options.text: Jonathan’s covenant with David.
options.note: The covenant is not presented as the spark for Saul’s jealousy; the song is.

options.text: David’s request for a larger command.
options.note: David made no such request; Saul himself gave David command, and jealousy arose from the song, not any request.

quiz.q: According to the chapter, why was Saul afraid of David?

options.text: Because the LORD was with David but had departed from Saul.
options.note: Verse 12 states this explicitly as the reason for Saul’s fear.

options.text: Because David commanded more soldiers than Saul.
options.note: David’s command grew, but the text names the LORD’s presence, not troop numbers, as the reason for Saul’s fear.

options.text: Because David refused to obey Saul’s orders.
options.note: David consistently obeyed and succeeded in what Saul sent him to do; disobedience is not the issue.

options.text: Because the Philistines had turned against Saul.
options.note: The Philistines are not described as opposing Saul directly here; his fear is of David, rooted in the LORD’s presence.

quiz.q: Why did the bride price of a hundred Philistine foreskins actually serve Saul’s scheme?

options.text: Saul intended for David to die at the hands of the Philistines while fulfilling the dowry.
options.note: Verse 25 states plainly that Saul intended to cause David’s death by the Philistines this way.

options.text: Saul wanted to test David’s courage before the wedding.
options.note: There was a real test of valor involved, but the text is explicit that Saul’s underlying motive was David’s death, not simply proving courage.

options.text: Saul wanted to strengthen ties with the Philistines.
options.note: The demand targeted Philistines as enemies to be struck down, not allies to befriend.

options.text: Saul had no ulterior motive in the request.
options.note: The text explicitly names Saul’s murderous intent behind the request.

quiz.q: What is the ongoing refrain that interprets David’s success throughout the chapter?

options.text: That the LORD was with David.
options.note: This phrase recurs at verses 12, 14, and 28, framing every success as God’s doing, not merely David’s skill.

options.text: That David was more skilled in battle than anyone else.
options.note: David’s skill is evident, but the text repeatedly credits the LORD’s presence as the deeper cause.

options.text: That the people always sided with whoever won the last battle.
options.note: The people’s love for David is noted, but it is presented as a response to God’s blessing on him, not mere crowd loyalty.

options.text: That Saul secretly favored David the whole time.
options.note: The opposite is true; Saul grew increasingly hostile even as David’s success continued.

quiz.q: How does Jonathan’s covenant with David point toward Christ?

options.text: The rightful heir freely yields his own claim and gives himself for the one God has chosen, foreshadowing Christ’s self-emptying love.
options.note: This mirrors Philippians 2:5-8, where Christ, the true heir, empties Himself for others rather than grasping His own glory.

options.text: It shows that royal succession never really mattered in Israel.
options.note: Succession mattered a great deal, which is exactly what makes Jonathan’s surrender of his claim so striking and costly.

options.text: It proves that Jonathan doubted David’s calling.
options.note: The covenant and the gift of his robe show confident recognition of David’s place, not doubt.

options.text: It has no meaningful connection to the gospel.
options.note: The self-giving pattern of a rightful heir yielding his claim genuinely foreshadows Christ’s own self-emptying love.

questions: Jonathan gave up his own claim to the throne out of love for David and trust in God’s choice. What claims or privileges is God asking you to release for the sake of someone else?
Saul’s jealousy grew from a single song, yet it hardened into a lifelong hostility. Where do you notice small comparisons or resentments starting to take root in your own heart?
The chapter repeats that the LORD was with David through danger, not around it. How does it change your view of hard seasons to know God’s presence does not mean the absence of opposition?
David kept serving faithfully even while Saul plotted against him. What would it look like for you to keep doing the next faithful thing while trusting God with an unresolved threat or conflict?
Jonathan’s covenant love cost him something real, his own robe and claim. Who in your life might need that kind of costly, self-giving loyalty from you this week?

translationNotes.note: The souls of Jonathan and David were knit together renders vivid Hebrew soul language for deep, bonded affection; it describes the closest kind of loyal friendship, not merely warm feeling.

Kept a jealous eye renders a Hebrew idiom of watching with suspicion and envy; the same root elsewhere describes zeal for the LORD, showing how the same intensity of heart can turn toward good or corrosive ends.

A spirit of distress renders a phrase the BSB footnote also gives as a harmful spirit; whichever nuance, the text is clear this affliction came upon Saul only after the LORD’s Spirit had departed from him, chapter 16:14.
